records.title: The Fresnel equations: one interface
records.summary: Reflection and transmission of a plane wave at a single planar interface: Snell's law, the Fresnel coefficients for s and p polarization, the Brewster angle and total internal reflection.

references.cite: M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.5
J. D. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 1999), §7.3–7.4
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
Every thin-film calculation is built from one event repeated: a plane wave meets a flat boundary between two
homogeneous media and splits into a reflected and a transmitted wave. Everything in this chapter follows from the
continuity of the tangential components of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ at that boundary.

## Snell's law

A wave in medium 1 (index $n_1$) arrives at angle $\theta_1$ from the normal. The tangential component of its wave
vector is the same on both sides, which fixes the direction of the transmitted wave:

$$
n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2 .
$$

The quantity $n \sin\theta$ is conserved through any stack of parallel layers, which is why a multilayer can be solved
layer by layer at a single in-plane wave number.

## Two polarizations, two sets of coefficients

The field is split into the part polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence (**s**, or TE) and the part
polarized in it (**p**, or TM). They do not mix at a planar interface. With $\cos\theta_2$ taken from Snell's law,
the amplitude coefficients are

$$
r_s = \frac{n_1\cos\theta_1 - n_2\cos\theta_2}{n_1\cos\theta_1 + n_2\cos\theta_2},
\qquad
r_p = \frac{n_2\cos\theta_1 - n_1\cos\theta_2}{n_2\cos\theta_1 + n_1\cos\theta_2},
$$

$$
t_s = \frac{2 n_1\cos\theta_1}{n_1\cos\theta_1 + n_2\cos\theta_2},
\qquad
t_p = \frac{2 n_1\cos\theta_1}{n_2\cos\theta_1 + n_1\cos\theta_2}.
$$

The sign of $r_p$ depends on the convention for the direction of the p field; this one follows Byrnes (2016), whose
transfer-matrix code PyStratify's planar engine extends. The power coefficients are

$$
R = |r|^2, \qquad T = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_2\cos\theta_2)}{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_1\cos\theta_1)}\,|t|^2 \;\;(s),
\qquad T = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_2\cos\theta_2^{*})}{\mathrm{Re}\,(n_1\cos\theta_1^{*})}\,|t|^2 \;\;(p),
$$

and $R + T = 1$ when neither medium absorbs. At normal incidence both polarizations reduce to
$R = \left(\frac{n_2 - n_1}{n_2 + n_1}\right)^2$: 4 % for glass in air.

::: example fresnel-air-glass

## The Brewster angle

$r_p$ vanishes when the reflected and transmitted directions are perpendicular. The dipoles driven in medium 2 would
then have to radiate along their own axis, which they cannot. This happens at

$$
\tan\theta_B = \frac{n_2}{n_1},
$$

56.3° for glass in air. Light reflected at the Brewster angle is purely s-polarized, which is how polarizing filters
cut glare and how Brewster windows keep a laser cavity lossless for one polarization.

## Total internal reflection

From the dense side ($n_1 > n_2$), Snell's law has no real solution beyond the critical angle

$$
\sin\theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}.
$$

There $\cos\theta_2$ becomes imaginary: the transmitted field decays exponentially away from the interface instead of
propagating, $|r_s| = |r_p| = 1$, and all the power is reflected. The evanescent field still reaches a fraction of a
wavelength into the second medium. A second dense medium brought that close lets light tunnel through (frustrated
total reflection), and a metal film there couples it to surface plasmons, the principle of the Kretschmann
configuration.

::: example fresnel-glass-air

## Absorbing media

For an absorbing medium the index is complex, $\tilde n = n + ik$ (time dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$), and so is
$\cos\theta_2$. The square root then has two branches; the physical one is the wave that carries power away from the
interface and decays into the medium. PyStratify chooses that branch for every layer, which is what keeps the
formulas above valid for metals, semiconductors above their band gap, and evanescent waves alike.

records.title: The transfer matrix: a stack of thin films
records.summary: Abelès' characteristic matrix of a layer, how a stack multiplies them, the admittance that gives R and T, and the quarter-wave and half-wave layers that coating design is built on.

references.cite: F. Abelès, Ann. Phys. (Paris) 12, 596 (1950)
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 2
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.6
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
Between two interfaces a wave travels back and forth, picking up phase on each pass, and every reflection spawns
another. Summing those multiple reflections term by term is possible for one layer, but impractical for twenty. The
transfer matrix does the bookkeeping instead: in each layer the field is a forward and a backward wave, and a $2\times
2$ matrix carries the two amplitudes, or the tangential fields, from one side of the layer to the other.

## The characteristic matrix of a layer

In layer $j$, of index $n_j$ and thickness $d_j$, the phase thickness at vacuum wavelength $\lambda$ is

$$
\delta_j = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\, n_j d_j \cos\theta_j ,
$$

with $\theta_j$ from Snell's law. The tangential electric and magnetic fields at the layer's two faces are related by
Abelès' characteristic matrix

$$
\begin{pmatrix} E \\ H \end{pmatrix}_{\text{front}} =
\begin{pmatrix} \cos\delta_j & \dfrac{i}{\eta_j}\sin\delta_j \\[4pt] i\,\eta_j \sin\delta_j & \cos\delta_j \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} E \\ H \end{pmatrix}_{\text{back}},
$$

where $\eta_j$ is the layer's tilted admittance, in units of the admittance of free space:
$\eta_j = n_j\cos\theta_j$ for s polarization and $\eta_j = n_j/\cos\theta_j$ for p.

## A stack and its admittance

Because the tangential fields are continuous at every interface, the matrices of successive layers simply multiply.
For $q$ layers on a substrate of admittance $\eta_s$,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} B \\ C \end{pmatrix} = \left(\prod_{j=1}^{q} M_j\right) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \eta_s \end{pmatrix},
\qquad Y = \frac{C}{B},
$$

and the whole stack behaves like a single surface of admittance $Y$ seen from the incident medium $\eta_0$:

$$
r = \frac{\eta_0 - Y}{\eta_0 + Y}, \qquad R = |r|^2, \qquad
T = \frac{4\,\eta_0\,\mathrm{Re}\,\eta_s}{|\eta_0 B + C|^2}.
$$

PyStratify's planar engine uses the equivalent form in amplitudes (an interface matrix and a propagation matrix per
layer, after Byrnes 2016), which also returns the fields inside the stack and the power absorbed in each layer.

## Quarter waves and half waves

Two thicknesses make the matrix trivial at the design wavelength $\lambda_0$, at normal incidence:

- a **half-wave** layer ($n d = \lambda_0/2$, $\delta = \pi$) has $M = -I$: it is *absent*, and the stack reflects
  as if it were not there;
- a **quarter-wave** layer ($n d = \lambda_0/4$, $\delta = \pi/2$) turns an admittance $Y$ into $n^2/Y$.

A single quarter-wave layer of index $n_1$ on a substrate $n_s$ therefore gives

$$
R = \left(\frac{n_0 n_s - n_1^2}{n_0 n_s + n_1^2}\right)^2 ,
$$

which vanishes for $n_1 = \sqrt{n_0 n_s}$, 1.23 for glass in air. No durable material has so low an index; magnesium
fluoride (1.38) comes closest, and leaves about 1.3 % instead of 4 %.

::: example quarter-wave-ar

The minimum sits at $\lambda_0 = 4 n_1 d$ and is broad, because $\delta$ changes slowly with $\lambda$. Two or three
layers (the V-coat and the quarter–half–quarter design) broaden it further; the
[tutorials](tutorials.html) build several such coatings.

## Oblique incidence and absorbing layers

Nothing above assumes normal incidence or real indices: at an angle, $\cos\theta_j$ shortens each layer's phase
thickness and the admittances differ between s and p. In an absorbing layer $\delta_j$ is complex and the wave decays
across it. For a thick metal or an evanescent layer the growing exponential in the matrix elements can exceed floating
point range; amplitude formulations that propagate decaying waves only avoid that.

records.title: Coherence and thick substrates
records.summary: Why a thin film draws interference fringes and a millimetre-thick substrate does not: the coherence length, the incoherent sum of intensities, and how a stack mixes coherent and incoherent layers.

references.cite: C. C. Katsidis and D. I. Siapkas, Appl. Opt. 41, 3978 (2002)
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §7.6
S. J. Byrnes, Multilayer optical calculations, arXiv:1603.02720 (2016)

records.body:
The transfer matrix adds amplitudes: every reflected wave interferes with every other. That is right for a film a few
hundred nanometres thick, and wrong for the glass it sits on. A 1 mm plate in a spectrometer shows no fringes, though
the matrix predicts them.

## Fringes too fine to see

Two reflections that differ by a path $2 n d \cos\theta$ interfere only if the light stays coherent over that path.
A source of bandwidth $\Delta\lambda$ has a coherence length

$$
\ell_c \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{\Delta\lambda}.
$$

Put the other way, the fringes of a slab are spaced by

$$
\Delta\lambda_\text{fringe} = \frac{\lambda^2}{2 n d \cos\theta},
$$

which for 1 mm of glass at 600 nm is 0.12 nm. Any instrument with a coarser resolution, nearly all of them, averages
over many fringes and records their mean. Real plates also vary in thickness by more than a wavelength across the beam,
which averages the phase just as well.

## Adding intensities

When the phase is averaged out, the multiply reflected waves add in power, not amplitude. For a bare, non-absorbing
plate with face reflectance $R_0 = \left(\frac{n - 1}{n + 1}\right)^2$, the geometric series gives

$$
R = R_0 + \frac{(1 - R_0)^2 R_0}{1 - R_0^2} = \frac{2R_0}{1 + R_0}, \qquad T = \frac{1 - R_0}{1 + R_0} ,
$$

8.2 % and 91.8 % for glass: twice the single-surface loss, less a little.

## Coherent films on incoherent plates

Katsidis and Siapkas (2002) generalised this to any stack: the layers are grouped into coherent sub-stacks, each
solved with the transfer matrix of amplitudes, and joined through incoherent layers by $2 \times 2$ matrices of
intensities. A thin film on a thick substrate is then exact for both: the film's fringes survive, and the substrate
contributes its two faces in power. PyStratify's planar engine implements this scheme; in the calculator each layer
carries a coherence flag (*c* or *i*), and the substrate behind the last layer is semi-infinite.

::: example film-on-thick-glass

At the film's half-wave wavelength it is absent, and the reflectance returns to the bare plate's $2R_0/(1 + R_0)$.
Between those points the film's fringes ride on the plate's incoherent
background, which is what a measured spectrum looks like.

## Partial coherence

Between the two limits sit rough interfaces, thickness gradients and finite spectral resolution, which damp fringes
without removing them. Katsidis and Siapkas treat these as phase averaging within a layer;
[Classics](classics.html#katsidis-2002) opens their coherent and incoherent wafer of Fig. 2 in the calculator.

records.title: Bragg mirrors: periodic stacks and stop bands
records.summary: A quarter-wave stack of two materials reflects almost perfectly over a band of wavelengths: the peak reflectance from the admittance, the stop band from the Bloch condition, and how contrast and period count set both.

references.cite: P. Yeh, A. Yariv and C.-S. Hong, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 67, 423 (1977)
H. A. Macleod, Thin-Film Optical Filters, 3rd ed. (Institute of Physics Publishing, 2001), ch. 5
M. Born and E. Wolf, Principles of Optics, 7th ed. (Cambridge University Press, 1999), §1.6.5
Y. Fink et al., Science 282, 1679 (1998)

records.body:
Alternate a high index $n_H$ and a low index $n_L$, each a quarter wave thick at $\lambda_0$, and the reflections from
every interface return in phase. With enough periods the stack reflects nearly everything over a band around
$\lambda_0$: a dielectric mirror with no absorption, the basis of laser mirrors, distributed Bragg reflectors in
VCSELs and the one-dimensional photonic crystal.

## The peak: quarter waves in series

At $\lambda_0$ each quarter-wave layer maps an admittance $Y$ onto $n^2/Y$ (see
[the transfer matrix](learn/films/transfer-matrix.html)). Starting from the substrate $n_s$, a pair L then H
multiplies it by $(n_H/n_L)^2$, so $N$ pairs, high index outermost, present

$$
Y = \left(\frac{n_H}{n_L}\right)^{2N} n_s ,
\qquad
R(\lambda_0) = \left(\frac{n_0 - Y}{n_0 + Y}\right)^2 .
$$

$Y$ grows geometrically with $N$, so $1 - R$ falls geometrically: eight pairs of TiO₂-like and SiO₂-like layers
(2.3 and 1.45) already reach 99.84 %.

## The band: Bloch waves

An infinite periodic stack is solved by Bloch's theorem. With $M$ the characteristic matrix of one period, a wave
propagates through the crystal when $|\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,M| \le 1$ and decays when
$|\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{Tr}\,M| > 1$: there the Bloch wave is evanescent and a thick enough stack reflects it
completely. For a quarter-wave stack at normal incidence the decaying range, the **stop band**, has a full width in
the relative wavenumber $g = \lambda_0/\lambda$ of

$$
\Delta g = \frac{4}{\pi}\arcsin\!\left(\frac{n_H - n_L}{n_H + n_L}\right),
$$

about 0.29 for 2.3/1.45, or 524–702 nm around 600 nm. The width depends on the index contrast alone; the period count
only decides how close to 1 the reflectance gets inside it and how sharp its edges are. The same band repeats at
$\lambda_0/3$, $\lambda_0/5$, …, where the layers are three or five quarter waves thick.

::: example bragg-mirror

Outside the band the stack is nearly transparent, with ripples, one fewer minimum between bands than there are
periods. [Classics](classics.html#yeh-1977) opens Yeh, Yariv and Hong's 15-period GaAs/AlGaAs stack, where the 14
zeros and the closing of the TM gap at the Brewster angle can be counted.

## At oblique incidence

Tilting the beam shortens every layer's phase thickness, so the band moves to shorter wavelengths, and splits by
polarization: the p band narrows and closes at the Brewster angle of the H/L interface. Fink et al. (1998) showed that
with enough contrast a stop band survives for every angle and both polarizations, an omnidirectional reflector built
from dielectrics alone.

records.title: Mie theory: light scattered by a sphere
records.summary: How a plane wave scatters off a homogeneous sphere: the multipole expansion, the coefficients a_ℓ and b_ℓ from two boundary conditions per order, the efficiencies, and where the series can stop.

references.cite: C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 4
W. J. Wiscombe, Appl. Opt. 19, 1505 (1980)
A. Moroz, Ann. Phys. 315, 352 (2005)
A. I. Kuznetsov et al., Sci. Rep. 2, 492 (2012)

records.body:
A sphere of radius $a$ and refractive index $n_s$ sits in a host of index $n_h$, lit by a plane wave of vacuum
wavelength $\lambda$. Two numbers decide everything that follows: the **size parameter** and the **relative index**,

$$
x = \frac{2\pi n_h a}{\lambda}, \qquad m = \frac{n_s}{n_h}.
$$

Gustav Mie solved this problem exactly in 1908, to explain why colloidal gold is red, violet or blue depending on the
size of its particles. The same solution describes a raindrop, a silicon nanoparticle and a biological cell under an
infrared microscope.

## Fields as a sum of multipoles

In spherical coordinates the vector wave equation separates. The fields inside and outside the sphere become sums of
vector spherical harmonics, each labelled by an angular order $\ell = 1, 2, \dots$ (dipole, quadrupole, …) and by its
character: **electric** (transverse magnetic, TM) or **magnetic** (transverse electric, TE). The radial dependence of
every term obeys the spherical Bessel equation, a second-order linear equation, so in each region it is a combination
of two independent solutions. We use the Riccati–Bessel functions

$$
\psi_\ell(\rho) = \rho\, j_\ell(\rho), \qquad \xi_\ell(\rho) = \rho\, h^{(1)}_\ell(\rho),
$$

regular at the centre and outgoing at infinity respectively.

## Two boundary conditions per order

At $r = a$ the tangential components of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ are continuous. For each order $\ell$ and each
character this gives two linear equations in two unknowns, the same $2\times 2$ structure as a single interface of a
thin film. Solving them gives the scattering coefficients of a non-magnetic sphere (time dependence
$e^{-i\omega t}$):

$$
a_\ell = \frac{m\,\psi_\ell(mx)\,\psi_\ell'(x) - \psi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}{m\,\psi_\ell(mx)\,\xi_\ell'(x) - \xi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)},
\qquad
b_\ell = \frac{\psi_\ell(mx)\,\psi_\ell'(x) - m\,\psi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}{\psi_\ell(mx)\,\xi_\ell'(x) - m\,\xi_\ell(x)\,\psi_\ell'(mx)}.
$$

$a_\ell$ is the electric multipole of order $\ell$, $b_\ell$ the magnetic one. The resonances of the sphere live in the
denominators: where one nearly vanishes, its coefficient peaks and the sphere radiates strongly in that multipole. Add
shells and each interface contributes one more $2\times 2$ matrix; that is the transfer-matrix solution of the
multilayered sphere, and what PyStratify computes for any number of layers.

## Efficiencies

Dividing the cross sections by the geometric area $\pi a^2$ gives the efficiencies:

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} = \frac{2}{x^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)\left(|a_\ell|^2 + |b_\ell|^2\right),
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{ext} = \frac{2}{x^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}(2\ell+1)\,\mathrm{Re}\,(a_\ell + b_\ell),
$$

and $Q_\mathrm{abs} = Q_\mathrm{ext} - Q_\mathrm{sca}$. Each term of the sums is the share of one multipole, which is
how the calculator splits a spectrum into its electric and magnetic orders.

## A silicon sphere

Silicon has an index near 4 across the visible. Inside so dense a particle the wavelength shrinks to $\lambda/n_s$, and
when it becomes comparable to the diameter the field inside circulates: a loop of displacement current, the
**magnetic dipole** $b_1$. It is the lowest resonance of a high-index sphere, longer in wavelength than the electric
dipole $a_1$ that follows it, and it gives such particles their colours (Kuznetsov et al., 2012).

::: example si-sphere-mie

Move the radius from 50 to 135 nm and the magnetic dipole walks across the visible spectrum; the electric dipole and
then the magnetic quadrupole follow it at shorter wavelengths.

## Where the series stops

The sums converge once $\ell$ exceeds the size parameter by a few terms. Wiscombe's rule

$$
\ell_\mathrm{max} = x + 4x^{1/3} + 2
$$

is accurate for far-field quantities. For a high-index core the internal size parameter $|m|x$ matters as well, so
PyStratify, and the calculator through it, take the larger of the two.

## Two limits worth knowing

For a sphere much smaller than the wavelength ($x \ll 1$) only $a_1$ survives, and

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} \approx \frac{8}{3}\,x^4 \left|\frac{m^2 - 1}{m^2 + 2}\right|^2,
$$

Rayleigh's $\lambda^{-4}$ law. For a metal the denominator vanishes near $\varepsilon_s = -2\varepsilon_h$: that is the
localized surface plasmon of a small gold or silver particle. For a sphere much larger than the wavelength,
$Q_\mathrm{ext} \to 2$: the sphere removes twice the light that falls on its cross section, half by absorption or
reflection and half by diffraction around its edge.

records.title: Multipoles, directional scattering and the Kerker conditions
records.summary: Reading a spectrum by its electric and magnetic multipoles: each order's share of the scattering, how a magnetic dipole arises in a dielectric, and how two multipoles interfering in phase cancel the backscattering.

references.cite: C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles (Wiley, 1983), ch. 4
M. Kerker, D.-S. Wang and C. L. Giles, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 73, 765 (1983)
A. I. Kuznetsov et al., Sci. Rep. 2, 492 (2012)
Y. H. Fu et al., Nat. Commun. 4, 1527 (2013)
A. E. Miroshnichenko et al., Nat. Commun. 6, 8069 (2015)

records.body:
The Mie series is a sum over multipoles, and every term has a physical identity: $a_\ell$ is the electric multipole
of order $\ell$ (dipole, quadrupole, …), $b_\ell$ the magnetic one. Taking a spectrum apart term by term turns a
curve with many bumps into a short list of resonances, each with its own field pattern and its own radiation
diagram.

## Each order's share

Because the vector spherical harmonics are orthogonal over the sphere, the scattered power is a plain sum over orders
and types, with no cross terms:

$$
Q_\mathrm{sca} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} \left(Q^{E}_{\ell} + Q^{M}_{\ell}\right),
\qquad
Q^{E}_{\ell} = \frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)\,|a_\ell|^2,
\qquad
Q^{M}_{\ell} = \frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)\,|b_\ell|^2 .
$$

Each term is bounded: a single channel cannot scatter more than $\frac{2}{x^2}(2\ell+1)$, the limit reached when
$|a_\ell| = 1$. Extinction splits the same way, through $\mathrm{Re}\,a_\ell$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,b_\ell$.

## A magnetic dipole without magnetism

Silicon has $\mu = 1$, yet a silicon sphere has a strong magnetic-dipole resonance. When the wavelength inside the
particle, $\lambda/n$, is close to its diameter, the electric field inside circulates around an axis perpendicular to
the incident field. That loop of displacement current is a magnetic dipole, and in a high-index sphere it is the
first resonance on the long-wavelength side. Kuznetsov et al. (2012) saw it move across the visible as the particles
grew, giving them their colours.

::: example si-sphere-multipoles

Move the radius and watch the order: magnetic dipole first, then electric dipole and magnetic quadrupole close
together, then the electric quadrupole. The electric dipole is broad because it also radiates from the particle's
polarization outside the resonance; the magnetic modes, confined inside the sphere, are narrower.

## Forward and backward

The far field in the forward and backward directions follows from the same coefficients:

$$
Q_\mathrm{f} = \frac{1}{x^2}\left|\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)(a_\ell + b_\ell)\right|^2,
\qquad
Q_\mathrm{b} = \frac{1}{x^2}\left|\sum_\ell (2\ell+1)(-1)^\ell (a_\ell - b_\ell)\right|^2 .
$$

Electric and magnetic multipoles of the same order add in the forward direction and subtract backwards. If only the
dipoles matter and $a_1 = b_1$, the backscattering vanishes: the **first Kerker condition**, found by Kerker, Wang and
Giles (1983) for spheres with $\varepsilon = \mu$. A silicon sphere reaches it where its electric- and magnetic-dipole
curves cross on the long-wavelength side of the magnetic resonance, and scatters forward almost only (Fu et al.,
2013). The **second Kerker condition**, $a_1 = -b_1$, minimises forward scattering, but cannot null it: the optical
theorem ties forward scattering to the extinction, which is never zero.

[Classics](classics.html#fu-2013) opens Fu et al.'s 150 nm silicon sphere with its scattering pattern; pick 660 nm to
see the forward lobe.

## Beyond the dipoles

When an electric dipole and a toroidal dipole of the same strength radiate in antiphase, their far fields cancel and
the electric-dipole scattering nearly vanishes while the field inside stays strong: the anapole (Miroshnichenko et al.,
2015). In the Mie picture it is simply a zero of $a_1$, visible in the decomposition as a dip of the electric dipole
between resonances.

import numpy as np
from pystratify import planar

verification.title: How PyStratify is verified
verification.summary: Every check behind multilayer.app's engine, geometry by geometry and source by source: closed forms, extended-precision references, independent methods, other groups' codes and published papers, each with its script, its tolerance and whether it runs on every test.
verification.body:
The calculator computes every film, cylinder and sphere with PyStratify, an open-source Python package (GPL-3.0).
This page lists what PyStratify is checked against. One row is one comparison: a reference, the quantity compared,
the script that runs it, the tolerance it must meet and whether the test suite asserts it on every change.

A check counts as independent only when the reference shares no code with PyStratify. Closed forms and conservation
laws are independent of any code; extended-precision references prove the numerics; another group's code or a
different method (finite differences in time, finite elements, boundary elements, volume integrals) proves the
formulation. Every comparison is a script in the PyStratify repository, so anyone can rerun it and see the numbers;
the rows marked *suite* run on every commit.

Rows the calculator can open show a worked example; the switch at the top shows one geometry at a time.

kinds.proves: a closed form, limit or conservation law: independent of any code
the same mathematics in mpmath at 60–80 digits, written separately in `src/pystratify/references.py` and `benchmarks/mp_reference.py`: proves the numerics, not the formulation
an independent formulation inside this repo (a scattering matrix, a plane-wave superposition, a quadrature): proves the formulation

a code that shares PyStratify's ancestry. `planar.py` *is* Byrnes's `tmm` (MIT notice in `src/pystratify/PLANAR-LICENSE.txt`); the backend's `inc_tmm`/"GTMM" path and the site's `tutorial-engine.js` descend from it. Agreement is a regression check only

statuses.meaning: asserted on every `pytest` run in this repo; rows marked "`benchmarks` extra" need `pip install -e ".[test,benchmarks]"` and run in the CI job `benchmarks`
scored per record by `harvester/verify.py`; not asserted
regenerated by `python benchmarks/convergence.py` into `RESULTS.md` (or `planar_codes.py` into `PLANAR_CODES.md`); not asserted
a `crosscheck/` script that writes CSV and PNG to lay over a published figure; agreement read by eye
not yet written; the row names what to compare and the tolerance to aim for
ruled out, with the reason in the row

verification.findings:
- **Where the remaining `to build` rows stand (2026-10-11).** Every code comparison PyStratify can run alone is
  built. What is left belongs elsewhere: the published-paper rows (OLED outcoupling, Davis 2010, Bohren &
  Huffman's cylinder, a nanowire emitter, FT-IR fibres and spheres, Oldenburg nanoshells and Kerker,
  Anger–Novotny quenching) are WP1.6 `crosscheck/` scripts, which the WP1.9 "seminal papers" plan
  (umbrella `docs/roadmap/showcase.md`) is building; pyElli 4×4, PyMoosh `anisotropic.py` and the isotropic
  limit wait for WP1.4's anisotropic solver; PyMoosh `non_local.py` waits for the `non-local` merge;
  OpenSANS needs its CPC program library download.

- **Films now have two independent codes** (2026-10-10): PyMoosh and pyElli agree with
  `pystratify.planar` to ≤ 1.2e-14 in R, T, r, t and per-layer A, and to ≤ 6e-13° in Ψ and Δ, including
  opaque and 20 µm absorbing layers, total internal reflection and a magnetic layer
  (`PLANAR_CODES.md`). Plane-wave fields agree with PyMoosh to ≤ 1.6e-14, and every guided mode of
  four lossless guides with PyMoosh (≤ 1.1e-11) and the slab dispersion relation (≤ 6.6e-14).
  Conventions that had to be mapped: PyMoosh's p-polarised t is the H-field ratio, and pyElli's
  Δ = 180° − Δ(tmm). Still open on films: anisotropy (pyElli's 4×4, with WP1.4).
- **Film emitter rates now have two outside references** (2026-10-10): independently written
  Sommerfeld integrals, pinned to the image-dipole closed form, agree with `FilmSource` to ≤ 5e-12;
  smuthi agrees on lossless guides to ≤ 4.8e-7. The guide comparison **found a bug**: a source in an
  exterior half-space lost all guided power (fixed in 0.10.3). **Cylinder emitters have an outside
  reference since 2026-10-10**: Meep's 3D FDTD converges toward PyStratify (0.74% at 60 px/µm, every
  orientation, through a mode cutoff), and its first run **found a bug**: the guided-mode search dropped
  real modes while reporting convergence (up to 12% here, 9.5% over random cylinders; fixed in 0.10.4,
  the found modes now equal the fibre's closed-form dispersion relations). NGSolve's 3D finite
  elements are the second volume method (1.5% at 0.8 µm; a mode just above cutoff needs a larger cell
  than 8 GB allows).
- **Volume methods (FDTD, FEM, BEM) are a different-method check at ~1%**, not a precision check:
  they test the formulation (sign conventions, normalisation, multipole bookkeeping), not the digits.
  Meep in cylindrical coordinates is cheap for a dipole on the symmetry axis: since 2026-10-10 a sphere
  agrees to 1.7% and a guiding film to 3.7% at 100 px/µm (2D, under a minute each); off-axis sources and
  cylinders need 3D runs, one at a time on this 8 GB Mac. At 200 px/µm Meep's E_z (m = 0) runs jump at the
  band's lowest frequency (+9% sphere, +12% film) while everything else keeps converging — Meep-side,
  noted in the report, not yet explained.
- **Spheres are the best covered**: precision, BHMIE, five papers, and since 2026-10-10 two Mie codes run
  publicly (scattnlay and treams agree with PyStratify to ≤ 1.8e-11 once 20 orders beyond Wiscombe's
  truncation are kept; at the default truncation, what a user gets, to ≤ 3.7e-8) and a
  different *method*: MNPBEM's boundary elements converge toward PyStratify for cross sections and
  decay rates (`MNPBEM_SPHERES.md`), and pyGDM2's volume dipoles agree within ~3% for dielectric
  spheres (`GDM_SPHERES.md`). A 5 nm nanoshell is beyond MNPBEM's affordable meshes here; three
  Mie codes (PyStratify, treams, scattnlay) settle that case exactly. **Near fields** too
  (2026-10-10): E and H inside every layer and outside agree with scattnlay to ≤ 8.2e-13 and the
  scattered field with treams to ≤ 6.6e-14; the centre is exact (Bohren & Huffman's d₁, c₁ to
  1e-14), where scattnlay loses up to 5e-3, and scattnlay's internal field fails toward the core of a
  10-layer sphere whose PyStratify coefficients agree with 60-digit transfer matrices. **Emitters**
  beside a sphere agree with smuthi to machine precision (2.2e-16) for dielectric spheres and to
  5e-10 for a metal-like sphere 5 nm away, converging with smuthi's truncation; beside **layered**
  spheres (a nanoshell, a matryoshka; electric and magnetic dipoles) with treams, to 3e-15 for
  dielectric shells and 3e-8 / 1e-11 for the metal ones; Meep (cylindrical coordinates) agrees to 1.7%.
- **Focused beams are verified only against their own plane-wave engines.** The FT-IR papers are
  the outside check.
- **The incoherent film path** has only the explicit phase average as an independent check. The
  backend's "GTMM" comparison is `inc_tmm` itself. PyMoosh's `incoherent.py` is now the outside
  check for a thick incoherent substrate; stacks with several incoherent layers are still unchecked.
- **PyMoosh covers the most planar cells of any one code**: R/T/A and fields, incoherent stacks,
  anisotropy, dipole sources, guided modes and hydrodynamic films. `benchmarks/planar_codes.py` is
  where its next cells go.
